verdicts.trueWording: Humans are notoriously bad at distinguishing human and LLM-generated text.
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext via Special:Export, revision 2026-09-06T13:13:42Z (matches 'version of 6 September 2026'). Section ==Caveats== / ===Your detection ability===. Quote exact; page adds 'a 2025 study has shown that human ability to distinguish LLM text from human is no better than random chance' (Cheng et al., Advances in Simulation). Both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: heavy users of LLMs can correctly determine whether an article was
verdicts.note: Same section. Page: 'A 2025 preprint has shown that heavy users of LLMs can correctly determine whether an article was generated by AI about 90% of the time... Study participants who didn't use LLMs much did only slightly better than random chance.' 'light users' is a fair paraphrase of 'didn't use LLMs much'. All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: these tools have non-trivial error rates
verdicts.note: Section ==Caveats== / ===AI detection tools===. Page: 'Do not solely rely on artificial intelligence content detection tools (such as GPTZero and Pangram)... these tools have non-trivial error rates. Detectors can be susceptible to factors such as text modifications (e.g. paraphrasing, markup, and spacing changes)...'. Every limb — GPTZero, Pangram, error rates, paraphrasing and markup — is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: all of its sensory language ends up getting attached to the immaterial
verdicts.note: NYT live URL returned HTTP 403; recovered via Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20251221211413id_/... which carries the full article body through the print footer ('Page 36 of the Sunday Magazine with the headline: The Omniwriter') — raw page reached, not a summary. Page: 'A.I. does still try to work sensory language into its writing, presumably because it correlates with good prose. But without any anchor in the real world, all of its sensory language ends up getting attached to the immaterial.' Directly follows the Woolf 'great plateful of blue water' passage, as the locator says.

verdicts.trueWording: In machine-written fiction, everything is spectral.
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture. Page: 'You'll notice, for instance, that A.I.s are absolutely obsessed with ghosts. In machine-written fiction, everything is spectral. Everything is a shadow, or a memory, or a whisper.' In the section beginning 'But if you task an A.I. with the production of culture itself', as the locator says. All limbs supported.

Page, immediately after the spectral passage: 'They also love quietness. For no obvious reason, and often against the logic of a narrative, they will describe things as being quiet, or softly humming.' Claim's 'the narrative' for the page's 'a narrative' is paraphrase outside the quoted text. All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: seven of those words were quiet, hum, humming, echo (twice!), liminal and ghosts
verdicts.note: Page: 'As evidence, the company's chief executive, Sam Altman, presented a short story it wrote... The story it produced was about 1,100 words long; seven of those words were "quiet," "hum," "humming," "echo" (twice!), "liminal" and "ghosts."' Every limb — Altman, evidence of creative writing, ~1,100 words, seven words, the exact list — is supported. The supplied quote is verbatim but sits one paragraph earlier than the locator implies: 'A.I.s are absolutely obsessed with ghosts' is in the preceding ghosts paragraph, not the Altman paragraph. Locator nit only; no claim limb affected.

Page: 'A lot of A.I.'s choices make sense when you understand that it's constantly tickling the Simpsons. The A.I. is trying to write well. It knows that good writing involves subtlety... So to reproduce the effect, it screams at the top of its voice about how absolutely everything in sight is shadowy, subtle and quiet.' Follows the ChatGPT-5 examples, as the locator says. All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: The technical term for this is “overfitting,”
verdicts.note: Page: 'The technical term for this is "overfitting," and it's something A.I. does a lot.' The antecedent 'this' is the preceding em-dash paragraph — the model drenching prose in a mark correlated with high quality in order to produce high quality — so the claim's characterisation (reproducing a marker instead of the quality) is exactly what the page names. Locator nit: the sentence introduces, rather than follows, the Simpsons tickling anecdote, which comes later in the same paragraph. No claim limb affected.

verdicts.trueWording: Within the A.I.’s training data, the em dash is more likely to appear
verdicts.note: Page: 'This might be the problem: Within the A.I.'s training data, the em dash is more likely to appear in texts that have been marked as well-formed, high-quality prose.' Both limbs supported. Recorded hedge: Kriss offers it as a candidate ('This might be the problem'), not a settled finding — the claim's 'Kriss's explanation' is fair, but do not restate it as established fact.

verdicts.trueWording: But it’s strangely hard to get rid of them.
verdicts.note: Page: 'But it's strangely hard to get rid of them. Users have complained that if you directly tell an A.I. to cut it out, it typically replies with something like: "You're totally right—em dashes give the game away. I'll stop using them—and that's a promise."' The quoted reply itself contains two em dashes, supporting the claim's final limb. Kriss relays it as a user report, which is what 'Kriss reports' asserts.

verdicts.trueWording: hundreds of Amazon books feature Elara Voss or Elena Voss
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim and the Elara Voss, Kael and pre-2023 limbs all hold: 'If you ask any A.I. to write a science-fiction story for you, it has an uncanny habit of naming the protagonist Elara Voss. Male characters are, more often than not, called Kael. There are now hundreds of self-published books on Amazon featuring Elara Voss or Elena Voss; before 2023, there was not a single one.' But the Amazon count is over Elara Voss OR ELENA VOSS — a female-name variant — not over Elara Voss and Kael. Kael appears nowhere in the Amazon sentence, so the claim's 'those names' overstates the page. Fix by writing 'Elara Voss or Elena Voss' for the Amazon figure and keeping Kael as a separate observation.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the hundreds of Amazon books use 'those names' including Kael — the page's pair is Elara Voss or Elena Voss

verdicts.trueWording: By 2024, usage had shot up by 2,700 percent.
verdicts.note: Page: 'In 2022, the word appeared in roughly one in every 10,000 abstracts collected in PubMed. By 2024, usage had shot up by 2,700 percent.' Both figures and the PubMed attribution are supported, and the section opens by crediting researchers who studied PubMed abstracts, matching 'reporting published research'.

verdicts.trueWording: A.I. is also extremely fixated on the rule of threes.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Second limb supported later in the same section: 'It's almost impossible to make A.I. stop saying "It's not X, it's Y" — unless you tell it to write a story, in which case it'll drop the format for a more literary "No X. No Y. Just Z."' The claim's 'in fiction' matches 'tell it to write a story'; 'not-X-but-Y' is a fair rendering of 'It's not X, it's Y'.

verdicts.trueWording: stopping midway through a sentence to ask itself a question
verdicts.note: Page: 'For instance, A.I. has a habit of stopping midway through a sentence to ask itself a question. This is more common when the bot is in conversation with a user, rather than generating essays for them.' Both limbs supported. The claim's word 'tic' is a paraphrase of the page's 'habit' (the article does use 'tic' for a sibling pattern nearby).
